claim: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed malignancy in women.
source: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed malignancy in women.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that cites established epidemiological knowledge about breast cancer incidence.

claim: Analysis of breast cancer genomic DNA indicates frequent loss-of-function mutations in components of the cJUN NH2-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling pathway.
source: Analysis of breast cancer genomic DNA indicates frequent loss-of-function mutations in components of the cJUN NH2-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling pathway.
evidence: This statement references prior genomic analyses of breast cancer, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Loss of JNK signaling caused genomic instability and the development of breast cancer.
source: Loss of JNK signaling caused genomic instability and the development of breast cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including exome sequencing and tumor incidence data.

claim: JNK deficiency caused widespread early neoplasia and rapid tumor formation in a murine model of breast cancer.
source: Moreover, JNK deficiency caused widespread early neoplasia and rapid tumor formation in a murine model of breast cancer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing MIN lesions and accelerated tumor formation in JNKKO mice.

claim: The tumor suppressive function of JNK was not mediated by a role in the growth of established tumors, but by a requirement to prevent tumor initiation.
source: This tumor suppressive function was not mediated by a role of JNK in the growth of established tumors, but by a requirement of JNK to prevent tumor initiation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing no difference in tumor cell proliferation, migration, or invasion in vitro, but increased early neoplasia in vivo.

claim: JNK pathway defects are 'driver' mutations that promote genome instability and tumor initiation.
source: Together, these data identify JNK pathway defects as 'driver' mutations that promote genome instability and tumor initiation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing genomic instability and tumor formation in JNK-deficient mice.

claim: Familial breast cancers result from germ-line mutations that increase the risk of cancer development.
source: Nevertheless, it is established that familial breast cancers result from germ-line mutations that increase the risk of cancer development (Afghahi and Kurian, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Examples of inherited mutations that can cause breast cancer predisposition include ATM, BRCA1/2, CDH1, CHEK2, NBN, and TP53.
source: Examples of inherited mutations that can cause breast cancer predisposition include ATM, BRCA1/2, CDH1, CHEK2, NBN, and TP53.
evidence: This is established knowledge about familial breast cancer genes.

claim: Sporadic mutation of ATM, BRCA1/2, CDH1, CHEK2, NBN, and TP53 and other genes promote the development of non-familial breast cancer.
source: Moreover, sporadic mutation of these and other genes promote the development of non-familial breast cancer (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established cancer biology literature.

claim: Changes in the tumor genome are important for breast cancer development.
source: Changes in the tumor genome are therefore important for breast cancer development (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established cancer biology principles.

claim: The sequencing of breast tumor genomic DNA has revealed mutations in genes that encode members of the JNK pathway, including MAP3K1, MAP2K4, and MAP2K7.
source: The sequencing of breast tumor genomic DNA has revealed mutations in genes that encode members of this pathway, including MAP3K1, MAP2K4, and MAP2K7 (Banerji et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Ciriello et al., 2015; Ellis et al., 2012; Kan et al., 2010; Nik-Zainal et al., 2016; Shah et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to genomic sequencing studies.

claim: The genetic changes in JNK pathway genes include frequent deletion of the gene locus and mutations that cause protein truncation and loss of protein kinase activity.
source: The genetic changes include frequent deletion of the gene locus and mutations that cause protein truncation and loss of protein kinase activity.
evidence: This is based on analysis of genomic data from cited studies.

claim: Breast cancer is associated with loss of JNK signaling.
source: This analysis suggests that breast cancer is associated with loss of JNK signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutation data cited in the manuscript.

claim: AKT phosphorylates and inactivates MAP2K4.
source: Indeed, since AKT phosphorylates and inactivates MAP2K4 (Park et al., 2002), breast cancer 'driver' mutations that activate AKT (e.g. PTEN and PI3K) also cause loss of JNK signaling.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Breast cancer 'driver' mutations that activate AKT (e.g. PTEN and PI3K) cause loss of JNK signaling.
source: Indeed, since AKT phosphorylates and inactivates MAP2K4 (Park et al., 2002), breast cancer 'driver' mutations that activate AKT (e.g. PTEN and PI3K) also cause loss of JNK signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited mechanism of AKT-mediated MAP2K4 inactivation.

claim: The JNK signaling pathway may be suppressed in many breast cancers.
source: The JNK signaling pathway may therefore be suppressed in many breast cancers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutation data and AKT-mediated inactivation mechanism.

claim: JNK1 (encoded by Mapk8) and JNK2 (encoded by Mapk9) isoforms exhibit partially redundant functions.
source: The JNK1 (encoded by Mapk8) and JNK2 (encoded by Mapk9) isoforms exhibit partially redundant functions (Davis, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Lactation induces Wap-Cre expression.
source: Lactation induces Wap-Cre expression (Wagner et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to the original Wap-Cre mouse publication.

claim: Cre-mediated recombination occurs in cytokeratin 8 (CK8) positive luminal epithelial cells.
source: Studies using Rosa26mTmG+/- female reporter mice demonstrated Cre-mediated recombination in cytokeratin 8 (CK8) positive luminal epithelial cells (Figure 1A), but not in cytokeratin 5 (CK5) positive myoepithelial cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Cre-mediated recombination does not occur in cytokeratin 5 (CK5) positive myoepithelial cells.
source: Studies using Rosa26mTmG+/- female reporter mice demonstrated Cre-mediated recombination in cytokeratin 8 (CK8) positive luminal epithelial cells (Figure 1A), but not in cytokeratin 5 (CK5) positive myoepithelial cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No breast cancer or pre-malignant mammary lesions were found in a cohort of 22 control MECRE mice.
source: We found no breast cancer or pre-malignant mammary lesions in a cohort of 22 control MECRE mice (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation of the mouse cohort.

claim: One palpable breast tumor (adenosquamous carcinoma) was identified in a 78 week old MEWT mouse.
source: However, studies of a cohort of 19 control MEWT mice identified one palpable breast tumor (adenosquamous carcinoma) in a 78 wk old mouse (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation documented in Figure 1C.

claim: Mammary intraepithelial neoplasia (MIN) was detected in one MEWT mouse during microscopic analysis.
source: In addition, mammary intraepithelial neoplasia (MIN) was detected in one MEWT mouse during microscopic analysis of tissue sections following necropsy.
evidence: This is based on histological examination of tissue sections.

claim: The incidence of palpable breast tumors in MEKO mice (31% of mice, median age 80 wk) was significantly greater than MEWT mice (p=0.037).
source: In contrast, the incidence of palpable breast tumors (31% of mice, median age 80 wk; p=0.037; Fisher's Exact Test) and MIN lesions detected at necropsy (41% of mice; p=0.0084; Fisher's Exact Test) in a cohort of 32 MEKO mice was significantly greater than MEWT mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of tumor incidence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The incidence of MIN lesions in MEKO mice (41% of mice) was significantly greater than MEWT mice (p=0.0084).
source: In contrast, the incidence of palpable breast tumors (31% of mice, median age 80 wk; p=0.037; Fisher's Exact Test) and MIN lesions detected at necropsy (41% of mice; p=0.0084; Fisher's Exact Test) in a cohort of 32 MEKO mice was significantly greater than MEWT mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of MIN incidence data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MEKO adenocarcinoma and adenosquamous carcinoma cells do not express JNK proteins.
source: Immunoblot analysis confirmed that the MEKO adenocarcinoma and adenosquamous carcinoma cells do not express JNK proteins (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: JNK deficiency promotes breast tumor development.
source: These data indicate that JNK deficiency promotes breast tumor development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the tumor incidence data presented.

claim: Both adenocarcinoma and adenosquamous carcinoma were detected in MEKO mice.
source: Microscopic analysis of tumor sections demonstrated the presence of adenosquamous carcinoma in MEWT mice, but both adenocarcinoma and adenosquamous carcinoma were detected in MEKO mice (Figure 1C,E,F).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figures 1C, E, and F.

claim: MEKO adenocarcinomas were primarily CK8 positive and variably expressed estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR).
source: The adenocarcinomas were primarily CK8 positive and variably expressed estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR), while the adenosquamous carcinomas expressed CK5 and did not express ER (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: MEKO adenosquamous carcinomas expressed CK5 and did not express ER.
source: The adenocarcinomas were primarily CK8 positive and variably expressed estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR), while the adenosquamous carcinomas expressed CK5 and did not express ER (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: CK8 expression by MEKO adenocarcinomas is consistent with a luminal epithelial cell origin.
source: CK8 expression by MEKO adenocarcinomas is consistent with both a luminal epithelial cell origin and the expression of Wap-Cre in luminal epithelial cells (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the CK8 staining data and the known expression pattern of Wap-Cre.

claim: CK5 expression by MEKO adenosquamous carcinomas suggests that these tumor cells may partially differentiate to express a marker of myoepithelial cells.
source: In contrast, CK5 expression by the MEKO adenosquamous carcinomas suggests that these tumor cells may partially differentiate to express a marker of myoepithelial cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the CK5 expression pattern observed.

claim: Exome sequencing of MEKO breast tumor cell lines demonstrated single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and short insertions/deletions (Indels).
source: This analysis demonstrated single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and short insertions/deletions (Indels) (Figure 1G), including high impact SNVs and Indels (frame-shifts and stop codons) within gene coding regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is based on exome sequencing data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Many chromosome segment amplifications and deletions (copy number variations, CNVs) were detected in MEKO tumor cells.
source: Moreover, many chromosome segment amplifications and deletions (copy number variations, CNVs) were detected (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on CNV analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Genomic instability is a consequence of JNK deficiency.
source: These data demonstrate that genomic instability is a consequence of JNK deficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the exome sequencing data showing mutations and CNVs in JNK-deficient tumors.

claim: RNA-seq analysis identified 2217 differentially expressed genes (q < 0.05, |log2 Fold Change| > 0.75) between MEKO tumor cells and primary mammary epithelial cells.
source: RNA-seq analysis identified 2217 differentially expressed genes (q < 0.05, |log2 Fold Change| > 0.75) that formed two clusters (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Both gene clusters identified in MEKO tumors were highly enriched for 'Pathways in Cancer'.
source: Pathway over-representation analysis using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database revealed that both clusters were highly enriched for 'Pathways in Cancer' (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on pathway analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: JNK deficiency caused reduced expression of AP1 transcription factors.
source: As expected, JNK deficiency caused reduced expression of AP1 transcription factors (Ventura et al., 2003) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Reduced expression of a 'DNA repair' gene signature was observed in MEKO tumor cells compared with primary mammary epithelial cells.
source: We also observed reduced expression of a 'DNA repair' gene signature (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) in MEKO tumor cells compared with primary mammary epithelial cells (MEC), consistent with the detection of accumulated mutations in MEKO tumor cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis identified a significant increase in 'WNT/β-Catenin Pathway' activity in MEKO tumor cells compared with MEC.
source: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) identified a significant increase in 'WNT/β-Catenin Pathway' activity in MEKO tumor cells compared with MEC (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on IPA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Increased expression of Wnt7b and Wnt10a was detected in MEKO cells compared with MEC.
source: Moreover, an enrichment of WNT signaling genes was found in the pathway over-representation analysis (Figure 2B, Cluster 2), including increased expression of Wnt7b and Wnt10a (Figure 2E) and increased expression of the WNT target genes Axin2, Ccnd1, and Myc in MEKO cells compared with MEC (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Increased expression of the WNT target genes Axin2, Ccnd1, and Myc was detected in MEKO cells compared with MEC.
source: Moreover, an enrichment of WNT signaling genes was found in the pathway over-representation analysis (Figure 2B, Cluster 2), including increased expression of Wnt7b and Wnt10a (Figure 2E) and increased expression of the WNT target genes Axin2, Ccnd1, and Myc in MEKO cells compared with MEC (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: MEKO tumors may exploit the WNT pathway during tumor development.
source: These data suggest that MEKO tumors may exploit the WNT pathway during tumor development.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed increase in WNT pathway activity.

claim: Loss of JNK on the TRP53-deficient background dramatically accelerated tumor formation.
source: Loss of JNK on the TRP53-deficient background dramatically accelerated tumor formation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on tumor-free survival data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The majority of JNKWT and JNKKO tumors were adenocarcinomas.
source: Histological examination of the JNKWT and JNKKO tumors confirmed that the majority of lesions were adenocarcinomas (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: JNKWT and JNKKO tumors presented with variable ER and PR staining patterns.
source: JNKWT and JNKKO tumors presented with variable ER and PR staining patterns (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cells primarily expressed the luminal marker CK8.
source: Moreover, both JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cells primarily expressed the luminal marker CK8, consistent with a luminal epithelial cell origin, although some dispersed cells did express the myoepithelial cell marker CK5 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No differences in PCNA staining were detected between JNKKO and JNKWT tumors, indicating that JNKKO tumors were not more proliferative than JNKWT tumors.
source: No differences were detected in PCNA-stained sections, indicating that JNKKO tumors were not more proliferative than JNKWT tumors (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on PCNA immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No differences in cleaved caspase 3 staining were detected between JNKWT and JNKKO tumors.
source: Similarly, we did not detect differences in cleaved caspase 3 staining between JNKWT and JNKKO tumors (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on cleaved caspase 3 immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: JNK deficiency causes significantly accelerated disease progression without greatly changing the tumor phenotype.
source: Collectively, these data show that JNK deficiency causes significantly accelerated disease progression without greatly changing the tumor phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the tumor formation kinetics and phenotypic analysis.

claim: Chromosome six was amplified and no chromosome was consistently deleted in JNKWT tumor cells.
source: CNV analysis demonstrated that chromosome six was amplified and no chromosome was consistently deleted in JNKWT tumor cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on CNV analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Chromosome six was amplified in some (two of six) JNKKO tumor cells.
source: Chromosome six was also amplified in some (two of six) JNKKO tumor cells (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on CNV analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The Kras locus was recurrently amplified in JNKWT tumor cells.
source: The proto-oncogene Kras resides on chromosome six and CNV analysis demonstrated that the Kras locus was recurrently amplified in JNKWT tumor cells (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) and was more highly expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on CNV analysis shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, and expression data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Kras was more highly expressed in JNKWT tumor cells compared to JNKKO tumor cells.
source: The proto-oncogene Kras resides on chromosome six and CNV analysis demonstrated that the Kras locus was recurrently amplified in JNKWT tumor cells (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) and was more highly expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Increased expression of a 'KRAS signaling' gene signature was detected in both JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cells.
source: Indeed, increased expression of a 'KRAS signaling' gene signature was detected in both JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: JNK deficiency selectively alters a subset of tumor-associated gene expression.
source: These data indicate that JNK deficiency selectively alters a subset of tumor-associated gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNA-seq analysis comparing different tumor genotypes.

claim: JNKWT tumor cells have a functional JNK signaling pathway, including stress-induced phosphorylation of both JNK and cJUN.
source: Studies of JNKWT tumor cells demonstrated the presence of a functional JNK signaling pathway, including stress-induced phosphorylation of both JNK and cJUN (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: JNK was not detected in JNKKO tumor cells.
source: However, JNK was not detected in JNKKO tumor cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The activation state of other MAPK pathways (ERK and p38) and the AKT pathway were similar between JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cells.
source: The activation state of other MAPK pathways (ERK and p38) and the AKT pathway were similar between JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on immunoblot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: No evidence of increased mammosphere propagation by JNKKO tumor cells was obtained.
source: No evidence of increased mammosphere propagation by the JNKKO tumor cells was obtained (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is based on mammosphere formation assay data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: No enhanced sphere formation by MEKO tumor cells was detected.
source: Moreover, we did not detect enhanced sphere formation by MEKO tumor cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is based on mammosphere formation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: JNKWT and JNKKO mammospheres showed similar organization with peripheral CK5+ cells and central CK8+ cells.
source: Staining of agarose-embedded JNKWT and JNKKO mammospheres revealed a similar organization with peripheral CK5+ cells and central CK8+ cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining of mammospheres shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The expression of stem cell markers (Bmi1, Nanog, and Pou5f1) was not significantly different between JNKWT and JNKKO mammospheres.
source: Finally, the expression of stem cell markers (Bmi1, Nanog, and Pou5f1) was not significantly different between JNKWT and JNKKO mammospheres (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Differences in cancer stem cell activity do not account for the accelerated tumor formation by JNKKO mice compared with JNKWT mice.
source: This analysis does not support the conclusion that differences in cancer stem cell activity account for the accelerated tumor formation by JNKKO mice compared with JNKWT mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mammosphere assay data.

claim: No differences between JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cell proliferation were detected.
source: No differences between JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cell proliferation were detected (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: No difference in JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cell migration during wound healing was found.
source: Similarly, we found no difference in JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cell migration during wound healing (Figure 6B) or in response to a serum gradient (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on wound healing assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: No difference in JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cell migration in response to a serum gradient was found.
source: Similarly, we found no difference in JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cell migration during wound healing (Figure 6B) or in response to a serum gradient (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cell invasion through matrigel-coated membranes was similar.
source: Moreover, JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cell invasion through matrigel-coated membranes (Figure 6C) and collagen I-filled wounds (Figure 6D) was similar.
evidence: This is based on transwell invasion assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cell invasion through collagen I-filled wounds was similar.
source: Moreover, JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cell invasion through matrigel-coated membranes (Figure 6C) and collagen I-filled wounds (Figure 6D) was similar.
evidence: This is based on collagen invasion assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: JNK deficiency does not alter breast tumor cell proliferation, invasion, or migration.
source: These data demonstrate that JNK deficiency does not alter breast tumor cell proliferation, invasion, or migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in vitro assay data.

claim: No differences between the growth of JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cells in orthotopically transplanted syngeneic mice were found.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, we found no differences between the growth of JNKWT and JNKKO tumor cells in orthotopically transplanted syngeneic mice (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This is based on orthotopic transplantation data shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: JNKKO tumor cells formed more colonies than JNKWT tumor cells when grown in soft agar.
source: Thus, JNKKO tumor cells formed more colonies than JNKWT tumor cells when grown in soft agar (Figure 6H,I) and JNKKO cells exhibited greater resistance to anoikis than JNKWT tumor cells (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is based on soft agar colony formation assay data shown in Figure 6H,I.

claim: JNKKO cells exhibited greater resistance to anoikis than JNKWT tumor cells.
source: Thus, JNKKO tumor cells formed more colonies than JNKWT tumor cells when grown in soft agar (Figure 6H,I) and JNKKO cells exhibited greater resistance to anoikis than JNKWT tumor cells (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is based on anoikis assay data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: JNK deficiency can promote tumor cell survival.
source: These data indicate that JNK deficiency can promote tumor cell survival.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the soft agar and anoikis assay data.

claim: JNKWT mice presented normal mammary gland morphology at 18 weeks after gene ablation.
source: JNKWT mice presented normal mammary gland morphology (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Multifocal mammary intraepithelial neoplasia (MIN) was observed in JNKKO glands at 18 weeks after gene ablation.
source: In contrast, multifocal mammary intraepithelial neoplasia (MIN) was observed in JNKKO glands (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The presence of MIN lesions in young JNKKO mice indicates that JNK-deficient mammary epithelial cells exhibit defects in apical-basal polarity.
source: The presence of MIN lesions in young JNKKO mice indicates that JNK-deficient mammary epithelial cells exhibit defects in apical-basal polarity, a hallmark of mammary tumor development (Halaoui et al., 2017; Zhan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the MIN lesion data and cited literature on polarity defects in tumor development.

claim: JNKKO epithelial cells showed increased proliferation compared with JNKWT epithelial cells in vivo.
source: Moreover, it is likely that mammary tumor development is further promoted by the increased survival of JNKKO cells in vitro (Figure 6H–J) and increased proliferation of JNKKO epithelial cells compared with JNKWT epithelial cells in vivo (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is based on PCNA staining data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: One physiological function of JNK in mammary epithelial cells is to suppress breast cancer development by preventing the initiation of carcinogenesis.
source: These data indicate that one physiological function of JNK in mammary epithelial cells is to suppress breast cancer development by preventing the initiation of carcinogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the early neoplasia data.

claim: The frequent mutation of the JNK pathway in human breast cancer implicates reduced JNK signaling in the etiology of mammary carcinoma.
source: The frequent mutation of the JNK pathway in human breast cancer (including the genes MAP3K1, MAP2K4, and MAP2K7) implicates reduced JNK signaling in the etiology of mammary carcinoma (Banerji et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Ciriello et al., 2015; Ellis et al., 2012; Kan et al., 2010; Nik-Zainal et al., 2016; Shah et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to genomic studies.

claim: Mutation of Mapk8 (encodes JNK1) and Mapk9 (encodes JNK2) is not frequently detected, most likely because of the functional redundancy of these JNK isoforms.
source: Mutation of Mapk8 (encodes JNK1) and Mapk9 (encodes JNK2) is not frequently detected, most likely because of the functional redundancy of these JNK isoforms (Davis, 2000).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known redundancy of JNK isoforms and the mutation frequency data.

claim: MAP2K4 and MAP2K7 serve as non-redundant activators of JNK and mutation of either MAP2K4 or MAP2K7 causes JNK inhibition.
source: In contrast, MAP2K4 and MAP2K7 serve as non-redundant activators of JNK and mutation of either MAP2K4 or MAP2K7 causes JNK inhibition (Tournier et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: MAP3K1 can act in a non-redundant manner to activate JNK.
source: Similarly, MAP3K1 can act in a non-redundant manner to activate JNK (Yujiri et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Tumor-associated ablation or mutation of MAP3K1, MAP2K4, or MAP2K7 causes JNK inhibition.
source: Tumor-associated ablation or mutation of these genes therefore causes JNK inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known functions of these genes in JNK activation.

claim: JNK signaling is inhibited by phosphorylation of MAP2K4 by AKT in breast tumors with AKT activation caused by 'driver' mutations in PTEN or PIK3CA.
source: Moreover, JNK signaling is also inhibited by phosphorylation of MAP2K4 by AKT (Park et al., 2002) in breast tumors with AKT activation caused by 'driver' mutations in PTEN or PIK3CA (Garraway and Lander, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Suppression of JNK signaling is a characteristic of many breast cancers.
source: Suppression of JNK signaling is therefore a characteristic of many breast cancers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutation data and AKT-mediated inhibition mechanism.

claim: Loss of JNK signaling in mammary epithelial cells caused breast cancer.
source: In contrast, we found that loss of JNK signaling in mammary epithelial cells caused breast cancer.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing tumor formation in MEKO mice.

claim: JNK deficiency accelerated tumor formation in a murine model of breast cancer.
source: Furthermore, JNK deficiency accelerated tumor formation in a murine model of breast cancer.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing accelerated tumor formation in JNKKO mice.

claim: The effects of JNK deficiency to promote tumor development were associated with widespread presence of early neoplasia and genomic instability.
source: These effects of JNK deficiency to promote tumor development were associated with widespread presence of early neoplasia and genomic instability.
evidence: This is based on the MIN lesion data and exome sequencing data.

claim: JNK plays a key role in the initiation of tumor development.
source: We show that JNK plays a key role in the initiation of tumor development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the early neoplasia data and lack of effect on established tumor growth.

claim: The frequent loss-of-function JNK pathway mutations in breast tumors represent 'driver' mutations that promote breast cancer development.
source: Thus, the frequent loss-of-function JNK pathway mutations in breast tumors represent 'driver' mutations that promote breast cancer development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that JNK deficiency promotes tumor formation.

claim: JNK loss plays a key role at the early stages of breast cancer development by promoting mammary gland neoplasia.
source: We find that JNK loss plays a key role at the early stages of breast cancer development by promoting mammary gland neoplasia (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on the MIN lesion data shown in Figure 7.

claim: JNK does not markedly influence the late-stage tumor phenotype.
source: In contrast to this tumor-suppressive role of JNK during early stages of carcinogenesis (Figure 7), JNK does not markedly influence the late-stage tumor phenotype (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on the lack of differences in tumor cell behavior in vitro and in orthotopic transplants shown in Figure 6.

claim: JNK does not change tumor cell proliferation, invasion or migration in vitro or tumor formation in orthotopically transplanted mice in vivo.
source: Thus, JNK does not change tumor cell proliferation, invasion or migration in vitro or tumor formation in orthotopically transplanted mice in vivo (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on the in vitro and in vivo assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: JNK deficiency represses tumor cell anoikis and promotes growth in soft agar in vitro.
source: However, JNK deficiency does repress tumor cell anoikis and promotes growth in soft agar in vitro (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on the anoikis and soft agar assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: JNK plays a major role in early tumor development, but only a minor role in established tumors.
source: JNK therefore plays a major role in early tumor development, but only a minor role in established tumors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of JNK deficiency on tumor initiation versus established tumor behavior.

claim: JNK deficiency has been shown to impair efficient epithelial cell death in response to cell detachment (anoikis) in vitro.
source: Indeed, JNK deficiency has been shown to impair efficient epithelial cell death in response to cell detachment (anoikis) in vitro and cause both occlusion of mammary ducts (Cellurale et al., 2012; Girnius and Davis, 2017) and delayed involution (Girnius et al., 2018) in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: JNK deficiency causes occlusion of mammary ducts in vivo.
source: Indeed, JNK deficiency has been shown to impair efficient epithelial cell death in response to cell detachment (anoikis) in vitro and cause both occlusion of mammary ducts (Cellurale et al., 2012; Girnius and Davis, 2017) and delayed involution (Girnius et al., 2018) in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: JNK deficiency causes delayed involution in vivo.
source: Indeed, JNK deficiency has been shown to impair efficient epithelial cell death in response to cell detachment (anoikis) in vitro and cause both occlusion of mammary ducts (Cellurale et al., 2012; Girnius and Davis, 2017) and delayed involution (Girnius et al., 2018) in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Both JNK and p38 MAPK promote mammary gland epithelial cell anoikis by a BIM-dependent mechanism.
source: For example, both JNK and p38 MAPK promote mammary gland epithelial cell anoikis by a BIM-dependent mechanism and are required for luminal clearance of mammary ducts (Cellurale et al., 2012; Girnius and Davis, 2017; Wen et al., 2011), but JNK inhibition promotes breast cancer (Figure 1 and 3) while p38 MAPK pathway inhibition suppresses breast cancer development and promotes the early dissemination of tumor cells (Del Barco Barrantes et al., 2018; Gawrzak et al., 2018; Harper et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: JNK and p38 MAPK are required for luminal clearance of mammary ducts.
source: For example, both JNK and p38 MAPK promote mammary gland epithelial cell anoikis by a BIM-dependent mechanism and are required for luminal clearance of mammary ducts (Cellurale et al., 2012; Girnius and Davis, 2017; Wen et al., 2011), but JNK inhibition promotes breast cancer (Figure 1 and 3) while p38 MAPK pathway inhibition suppresses breast cancer development and promotes the early dissemination of tumor cells (Del Barco Barrantes et al., 2018; Gawrzak et al., 2018; Harper et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: p38 MAPK pathway inhibition suppresses breast cancer development and promotes the early dissemination of tumor cells.
source: For example, both JNK and p38 MAPK promote mammary gland epithelial cell anoikis by a BIM-dependent mechanism and are required for luminal clearance of mammary ducts (Cellurale et al., 2012; Girnius and Davis, 2017; Wen et al., 2011), but JNK inhibition promotes breast cancer (Figure 1 and 3) while p38 MAPK pathway inhibition suppresses breast cancer development and promotes the early dissemination of tumor cells (Del Barco Barrantes et al., 2018; Gawrzak et al., 2018; Harper et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Anoikis defects and ductal occlusion by detached epithelial cells caused by stress-activated MAPK inhibition is not sufficient for tumor formation.
source: These data indicate that anoikis defects and ductal occlusion by detached epithelial cells caused by stress-activated MAPK inhibition is not sufficient for tumor formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of JNK and p38 MAPK inhibition on breast cancer.

claim: JNK deficiency caused genomic instability associated with widespread SNVs, Indels, and CNVs.
source: We found that JNK deficiency caused genomic instability associated with widespread SNVs, Indels, and CNVs (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on exome sequencing data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Genetic changes caused by JNK deficiency likely contribute to tumor development.
source: It is likely that these genetic changes caused by JNK deficiency contribute to tumor development.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed genomic instability.

claim: JNK-mediated phosphorylation of SIRT6 stimulates double-stranded DNA break repair.
source: Examples include JNK-mediated phosphorylation of SIRT6 to stimulate double-stranded DNA break repair (Van Meter et al., 2016) and JNK-mediated phosphorylation of DGCR8 to induce transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (Calses et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: JNK-mediated phosphorylation of DGCR8 induces transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair.
source: Examples include JNK-mediated phosphorylation of SIRT6 to stimulate double-stranded DNA break repair (Van Meter et al., 2016) and JNK-mediated phosphorylation of DGCR8 to induce transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair (Calses et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Loss of JNK signaling would be expected to cause defects in DNA repair that result in increased genomic instability.
source: Loss of JNK signaling would therefore be expected to cause defects in DNA repair that result in increased genomic instability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known roles of JNK in DNA repair.

claim: JNK deficiency in the mammary epithelium causes genomic instability and breast cancer.
source: Indeed, our analysis demonstrates that JNK deficiency in the mammary epithelium causes genomic instability (Figure 1G) and breast cancer (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on the exome sequencing and tumor incidence data.

claim: JNK deficiency may increase the sensitivity of tumor cells to drugs that cause DNA damage.
source: JNK deficiency may therefore increase the sensitivity of tumor cells to drugs that cause DNA damage.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed DNA repair defects in JNK-deficient cells.

claim: The TRP53 pathway is important for genome stability and tumor suppression.
source: The TRP53 pathway is known to be important for genome stability and tumor suppression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TRP53 function.

claim: The JNK pathway promotes genome stability and tumor suppression.
source: Our data demonstrate that the JNK pathway similarly promotes genome stability and tumor suppression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The number of SNVs and indels caused by TRP53 deficiency was greater than that caused by JNK deficiency.
source: The number of SNVs and indels caused by TRP53 deficiency was greater than that caused by JNK deficiency.
evidence: This is based on comparison of exome sequencing data from different genotypes.

claim: The number of CNVs were similar between TRP53-deficient and JNK-deficient backgrounds.
source: Nevertheless, the number of CNVs were similar on both genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This is based on comparison of CNV data from different genotypes.

claim: While both TRP53-deficiency and JNK-deficiency can cause genomic instability, the mechanisms engaged by these two pathways may be different.
source: These observations indicate that while both TRP53-deficiency and JNK-deficiency can cause genomic instability, the mechanisms engaged by these two pathways may be different.
evidence: This is speculation based on the different patterns of genomic instability observed.

claim: The JNK pathway can promote cell proliferation and survival through regulation of AP1 transcription factors.
source: For example, the JNK pathway can promote cell proliferation and survival through regulation of AP1 transcription factors (Das et al., 2007; Lamb et al., 2003; Ventura et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The JNK/JUN signaling pathway may promote the proliferation of some breast tumor cells in vitro.
source: Indeed, the JNK/JUN signaling pathway may promote the proliferation of some breast tumor cells in vitro (Guo et al., 2006; Xie et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: JNK signaling may have pro-oncogenic functions in certain tumor types or under specific conditions.
source: It is therefore possible that JNK signaling may have pro-oncogenic functions in certain tumor types or under specific conditions (Whitmarsh and Davis, 2007).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation.

claim: A major role of JNK signaling in the breast epithelium is tumor suppression.
source: Nevertheless, our analysis establishes that a major role of JNK signaling in the breast epithelium is tumor suppression (Figure 1 and 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The tumor suppressive role of JNK signaling is consistent with the discovery of frequent JNK pathway gene ablation and mutation in human breast cancer.
source: This role of JNK signaling is consistent with the discovery of frequent JNK pathway gene ablation and mutation in human breast cancer (Banerji et al., 2012; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Ciriello et al., 2015; Ellis et al., 2012; Kan et al., 2010; Nik-Zainal et al., 2016; Shah et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to human cancer genomic data.

claim: JNK deficiency in the mammary epithelium can cause murine breast cancer.
source: The major conclusions of this study are that: (1) JNK deficiency in the mammary epithelium can cause murine breast cancer; and (2) JNK deficiency rapidly accelerates tumor development in a mouse model of breast cancer.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: JNK deficiency rapidly accelerates tumor development in a mouse model of breast cancer.
source: The major conclusions of this study are that: (1) JNK deficiency in the mammary epithelium can cause murine breast cancer; and (2) JNK deficiency rapidly accelerates tumor development in a mouse model of breast cancer.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: JNK can act as a breast cancer tumor suppressor.
source: These observations indicate that JNK can act as a breast cancer tumor suppressor.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Frequent mutational inactivation of genes that encode JNK pathway components (e.g. MAP2K4 and MAP3K1) are detected in human breast cancer.
source: This is a significant finding because frequent mutational inactivation of genes that encode JNK pathway components (e.g. MAP2K4 and MAP3K1) are detected in human breast cancer (Garraway and Lander, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review of cancer genomics.
